value.0: Finished work stands in front of me. The temper is in you now the way it sits in good steel: invisible, and permanent. My forge has nothing left to teach you. Go be an anvil for somebody else.

You carry that heavy blade like a man still arguing with its weight. Steel argues back. Master the weapon end to end, every swing and every stance it has, and then stand in front of me again. Until then you're green stock, and I don't waste heat on green stock.

Your guard drops a finger's width every time you breathe out. That's a flaw in the grain, and flaws crack under load. The Forge Caverns below this rock can work it out of you. Smith-guards hold the galleries now, sworn to an oath I never approved, and their newest call themselves adepts. Cut down six adepts and bring me the Absolute Defense Forge Heat Ledger they keep by the crucibles. Do that, and I'll start hammering that flaw out of your guard.

Then we begin at the fire. The key I've just given you opens the sealed gate down into the Korriban Forge Caverns. Work the galleries steady, no hurry and no hesitation, and come back with the ledger while the heat of it is still in your hands.

A guard that has stopped pretending. Absolute Defense is steel tempered until nothing on the far side of it matters, a wall you carry in two hands. The forge heat is the only honest test I know. Flattery melts. Excuses burn off. What's left either holds or it doesn't, and down there you'll be tested the same way the steel is.

Smith-guards. Mine, once. They swore their edges to the forge, then quenched that oath in a darker one, some Sith doctrine promising steel that never yields to anything, loyalty included. Now they hold my lower galleries and run heats I never signed. The adepts are the greenest of them. Green steel still cuts.

Every heat in a lawful forge goes in the ledger. Temperature, time, whose hands worked the metal. Forge law says the ledger is the forge, and whoever holds it answers for every blade those galleries have produced. Bring me the Forge Heat Ledger and their work becomes mine to judge again.
The galleries are still working, which means you're not finished. Six adepts, and the Absolute Defense Forge Heat Ledger from beside the crucibles. Steel doesn't temper by being talked about.
You smell of slag and crucible smoke. Something came out of that fire with you. Show me.

Every heat they've run, signed in their own hands. Rushed quenches, sloppy tempers. I'd have broken half these blades over my knee. You held your guard against their steel and came back whole; that's the first pass of the hammer. There will be more heat next time.

The flaw in your breathing is smaller. Not gone. This ledger names five specialists, journeymen of their bad oath, the ones who run the tempering racks. They cool every new blade through a Sith device that whispers hunger into hot steel. Break the five and pull the Absolute Defense Sith Tempering Matrix out of the quench trough before it finishes another edge.
Good. You hold the gate key already; the racks sit deeper, past the first crucible hall, where the heat starts to talk. Keep your guard closed going down and closed coming back.

A Sith tempering matrix. It sits in the quench trough and murmurs while the steel cools, and the steel remembers what it hears. Blades that hold grudges. Edges that want. Forge law calls any unsanctioned temper a corruption of the stock, and I want that thing off my racks and cold in my hands.

The wrong fire at the wrong time, same as ruins most good steel. A Sith came down from the crypts preaching a defense that yields nothing, ever, to anyone. My smiths heard 'unbreakable' and stopped hearing anything else. Oaths are welds. Made in bad heat, they look solid right up until the day they shear.

There's one below the smith-guards call the master. I have watched his guard across three generations of steel and never once seen it passed. Not by me. Not by anyone I trained. You are not ready to talk about him, so we won't.
Five specialists still stand between you and the tempering rack. Come back when the Absolute Defense Sith Tempering Matrix is cold in your pack, not before.
Your pack is humming. That's the matrix wanting its trough back. Set it down slow.
Cold, and quieter already. You cut off their tempering and their journeymen in one heat. Second pass of the hammer. The grain in you is starting to close.

Now the work gets honest. The galleries answer to a warden, the anvil-keeper, the man who broke my last three apprentices without moving his back foot. His guard is this discipline done nearly right, and nearly is what makes him cruel. So hear me, because this is forge law and not caution: heavy work takes a crew at the anvil. One pair of hands cannot turn steel that size. Take a working crew down with you, two hammers at the least, or the warden will fold you into the floor like the others. Break him, and bring me the Absolute Defense Cracked Anvil Sigil he wears.

Then gather your crew before you touch that gate. I mean it. The warden has flattened finer steel than yours, one billet at a time, patient as rust. Strike as a crew, rest the guard in turns, and don't be proud about whose blow lands last.

He kept my anvils for twenty years. Best hammer-hand I ever trained, and the first to swear the bad oath. The night the galleries turned, he cracked his own anvil to mark it and kept a shard for a sigil. Understand: he doesn't attack. He waits, and lets you break yourself against him. The patience is the lesson. It's also the trap.

In forge law, the anvil is the forge's word. Crack one, and you've broken your word to every smith who ever worked it. He wears that crack proudly, like it set him free. Bring the sigil to me and his claim on my galleries cracks with it.

Because adepts and journeymen are not a warden. A heavy blade turning alone tires. A guard with no relief breaks. His whole doctrine counts on both. Three sets of hands means the pressure never rests and neither does he, and that isn't courtesy, it's the technique itself. A wall holds longest where the line behind it is more than one deep.
The warden still keeps the anvil, or you'd be talking less and breathing harder. Crew. Patience. Relief on the guard. And the Absolute Defense Cracked Anvil Sigil in my hand when he's down.
You're standing straighter under that blade's weight. The anvil has a new keeper, then. Show me.

So his guard could be passed after all. It took a crew, and that doesn't lessen the work; that is the work. Third pass of the hammer. The grain is nearly closed. Rest your hands, because the inner ring will not be gentler.

The warden was the wall. Behind the wall sits the inner circle: four overseers who sign the heats now, who taught the bad oath and grade it in my forge with my tools. They hold the deep floor in a ring around the master's anvil. Each carries stamped clearance. Bring me one Absolute Defense Overseer's Clearance Token, whole and unmelted, and I'll put their forgeries in front of forge law. Keep your crew close. Four overseers on their own floor is a fire, and you don't split up inside a fire.
You didn't flinch at four. That's temper showing. The deep floor burns hotter than the galleries, so work in short heats, watch each other's guard, and come up before the air goes bad.

Clearance to stand the deep floor and sign heats in the forge's name. They minted their own tokens, and that's forgery under any forge law older than Korriban. One genuine token in my hand turns every blade they've signed from armament into evidence.

Now you're ready to ask, so I'll answer. He holds the innermost ring, and he holds the finished thing itself: the guard you've been bleeding toward, whole, with no flaw left in the grain. When his circle falls he will know your name without being told. He reads footwork off the stone the way I read a heat off the color of the steel.

When you first stood here, your guard dropped a finger's width on the out-breath. It doesn't anymore. That's what honest heat does. It adds nothing to the steel; it burns off everything that was never steel to begin with. What's left of you rings when it's struck. One ring remains, and it isn't yours yet.
Four overseers still sign heats on my deep floor, so we are not finished. One Absolute Defense Overseer's Clearance Token. Whole. Unmelted. In my hand.
Deep-floor scale on your boots. The circle is broken, then. Let me see the token.

Genuine. Their signatures die with this stamp. Fourth pass of the hammer, and I notice I've stopped inspecting your guard and started learning from it. Strange feeling for an old overseer. One heat remains.

The innermost ring, then. The master holds it alone, and his guard is the finished discipline entire: the wall you've been building one pass at a time, already built, grown old and patient behind him. Hear this plainly. No one has ever passed that guard alone, and no one who went down without a crew came back up to complain about it. Take yours. Two hammers sworn to your rhythm at your back, at the least. Turn his patience against itself, spell each other on the pressure, and wait for the one breath he finally has to take. There's nothing to carry out when it's done. His fall is the proof, and the guard you walk out with is the prize.
Then this is the last heat. When the ring goes quiet, don't stand around admiring the anvil. Come up. I want to see what walks out of that fire, because I already know what walked in.

Alone? No. I've watched it my whole working life and I'd stake the forge on it. But the guard holds one arc at a time. That is its entire law, and its single seam. Three blades make three arcs, and his wall has to choose. Whatever it leaves open belongs to you. He knows this as well as I do. He's counting on your pride to send you down alone.

Look at my hands. Forty years of hammer and tong, and they'd still hold a blade. But he was my finest work before he was my failure, and a smith who quenches the same steel twice ruins it. It has to be new hands. It has to be yours.

The oath dies with the ring. Whoever's left below comes up and answers forge law, the heats get re-signed, and Korriban keeps one forge that makes blades instead of doctrine. And you walk out carrying the only guard that matters. Yours. Finished.
The master still holds the ring. Don't go down light. A crew, rested, and no pride about whose blow lands last. The fire will wait. It always does.
Quiet. The whole rock has gone quiet. Forty years I've listened to that ring and it was never once quiet. Tell me.

Then the flaw is out of the grain, the forge's and yours both. The guard isn't mine to grade anymore; you wear the finished temper now, and steel that finished doesn't answer to overseers. The work's done. The fire is yours.
Another question first.
Put me in the fire, then.
What is Absolute Defense, exactly?
Who holds these caverns?
What does this ledger prove?
Not yet. I know my flaws.
The Absolute Defense Forge Heat Ledger. Six adepts won't add to it again.
I have another question.
I'll pull it out of the trough myself.
What is this tempering matrix?
What turned your smiths?
Tell me about their master.
Not this heat. I'll be back.
The Absolute Defense Sith Tempering Matrix, cold as you asked.
One more thing before I go down.
I'll bring hands I trust to the anvil.
Who is this warden?
What is the sigil he wears?
Why a crew? I've held alone so far.
My crew isn't gathered yet.
The Absolute Defense Cracked Anvil Sigil, off the warden himself.
Before I go, a question.
Four overseers. Consider them worked.
What does the token clear, exactly?
I'm ready to ask about the master.
How does the steel look, overseer?
The deep floor can wait one more day.
One Absolute Defense Overseer's Clearance Token, taken whole.
Hold the heat. I have questions.
We'll take the ring together. I'll finish it.
Can his guard be passed at all?
Why send me? Why not go yourself?
And the forge, when he falls?
Not until my crew is rested.
The master's guard broke. The ring is quiet.
